title: Territory-dependent plasticity

html:
A crucial point, and one that follows directly from the parallel-loop architecture described in the loss- and error-signal sections, is that the striatum does not instantiate one uniform plasticity rule everywhere. The molecular primitives recur—glutamatergic coincidence, postsynaptic depolarization, dopamine, acetylcholine, endocannabinoids, and local inhibition—but the sign, timing sensitivity, dominant induction regime, and functional consequence of those primitives vary across striatal territories. Territory-specific plasticity is therefore not an incidental modulation layered atop a generic BG learning rule; it is one of the mechanisms by which the same dopaminergic evaluative variable is converted into different forms of policy optimization in associative, sensorimotor, limbic, and posterior striatal loops 1, 2, 3, 4. A rat study records dopamine across striatal regions (Figure).

Some of the clearest evidence comes from dorsomedial versus dorsolateral striatum. Perez and colleagues showed that corticostriatal STDP is itself region-specific: DMS expresses predominantly symmetric anti-Hebbian plasticity, whereas DLS expresses asymmetric anti-Hebbian STDP 1. Their modeling further showed that these two rules have different computational consequences: the symmetric rule favors memory flexibility and rapid updating, whereas the asymmetric rule favors memory maintenance, providing an unusually clean synaptic correlate of the canonical behavioral division in which DMS supports flexible goal-directed control and DLS supports the stabilization of habitual policies. Importantly, during motor-skill learning, plasticity in that study was engaged in DMS and in DLS striatonigral neurons during early learning, whereas DLS striatopallidal neurons were mobilized later, indicating that the locus of corticostriatal modification shifts across training rather than simply scaling uniformly with practice 1. The study compares reward-history timescales across the striatum (Figure).

This DMS-DLS asymmetry is not only descriptive; it plausibly changes what each territory is good at learning. Vignoud and colleagues showed that anti-Hebbian corticostriatal STDP, especially when combined with two classical striatal features–spike latency and collateral inhibition–is well suited for learning spike sequences, and explicitly note that realistic models will need to incorporate the experimentally observed distinction between DMS and DLS anti-Hebbian regimes 5. In that sense, a DMS-like rule appears well matched to continual policy revision and relearning, whereas a DLS-like rule appears well matched to the chunking and stabilization of repeated sensorimotor sequences into durable habits 5, 1. A recent striatal model links dopamine-dependent plasticity and direct/indirect pathway activity to action selection and reinforcement learning (Figure) 16.

Moving from the dorsal to the ventral striatum, the plasticity landscape changes again, in ways that may reflect the distinct computational demands of the limbic cortico-basal ganglia loops. Ji and Bhatt examined STDP in core nucleus accumbens (NAc) SPNs using spike-timing protocols that more closely approximated in vivo firing patterns than high-frequency stimulation 6. Relative to the classical anti-Hebbian rule often observed in dorsal striatal slice preparations under intact inhibitory conditions, the same anti-Hebbian pairing protocol (post-before-pre at low frequency) in NAc core SPNs evoked bidirectional long-term plasticity: roughly half of recorded SPNs underwent timing-dependent LTP and the other half underwent timing-dependent LTD, with the two outcomes appearing to segregate into functionally distinct neuronal subpopulations 6. Moreover, the molecular mechanisms underlying tLTP and tLTD in NAc differed from those in dorsal striatum: tLTP depended on NMDA receptors but not on action potentials (consistent with a purely dendritic induction mechanism), whereas tLTD required action potentials and calcium-induced calcium release from ryanodine-sensitive intracellular stores–a dependence on ryanodine receptors rather than IP3 receptors that contrasts with the dominant LTD mechanisms in dorsal striatum, where endocannabinoid- and IP3-dependent pathways predominate 6. Even the effects of dopamine receptor agonists on MSN firing diverged from dorsal striatal expectations: a subset of NAc MSNs whose firing was strongly suppressed by dopamine agonists was exclusively associated with tLTP, but the relationship between D1/D2 receptor expression and plasticity polarity was not as cleanly segregated as in dorsal striatum 6. These findings suggest that NAc core operates under a distinct plasticity regime in which bidirectional plasticity can be generated by a single induction protocol, potentially enabling rapid, flexible reweighting of cortico-accumbal synapses in response to motivational contingency changes. A 2025 mouse study examines prediction errors beyond reward (Figure) 17.

The cholinergic gating of plasticity is also territory-dependent. As described in the error-signal section, recent work suggests that the relationship between striatal cholinergic pauses and dopaminergic reward signals is not uniform across subregions 2. Complementing that systems-level observation, Marche, Martel, and Apicella showed that cholinergic interneurons (TANs) themselves display region-specific response properties in primates performing a Pavlovian conditioning task 7. In ventral (limbic) striatum, the fraction of TANs responding to reward was higher than in motor or associative dorsal striatum, and TAN pause responses were generally longer; for reward-predictive stimuli, pause magnitude was also greater in ventral than dorsal territories 7. Because corticostriatal LTP requires the coincidence of a cholinergic pause, phasic dopamine, and SPN depolarization 8, these ventral TAN dynamics may permit reward-related teaching signals to influence plasticity over a broader temporal window. This interpretation is broadly consistent with evidence that dopamine signals follow a ventral-to-dorsal striatal gradient of reward time horizons, with slower discounting in ventral striatum than in more dorsal territories 9. The regional TAN differences likely reflect differences in afferent organization, potentially including regionally heterogeneous midbrain dopamine/glutamate signaling, although the precise circuit basis remains unresolved 7, 10. A 2026 review illustrates local dopamine–acetylcholine interactions (Figure) 18.

Overlaying the ventral-to-dorsal territorial gradient is the striosome–matrix compartmental axis, which introduces a further dimension of plasticity heterogeneity. As established in the loss-function and error-signal sections, striosomes are disproportionately positioned to regulate dopaminergic teaching signals through their specialized projections to SNc dopamine neurons, whereas matrix SPNs are more tightly embedded in the canonical action-output channels 11. This anatomical distinction likely has corresponding plasticity consequences. Dopamine transmission itself differs across the two compartments: in dorsal striatal slice preparations, electrically evoked dopamine release is slightly higher in matrix than in striosomes, despite reports that dopaminergic axon density is greater in striosomes 12. More importantly, the modulatory effects of dopamine on SPN state transitions differ between compartments: D1 signaling prolongs dendritically evoked up states in matrix dSPNs while shortening them in striosomal dSPNs 13. This suggests that the same class of dopaminergic event could bias the temporal conditions for plasticity induction in opposite directions across the two compartments, though this remains an inference rather than a directly demonstrated learning-rate effect. Combined with evidence that striosomal neurons exhibit stronger representations of reinforcement outcomes—especially large reward and punishment prediction errors—than matrix neurons during cost-benefit foraging 14, and that in classical conditioning dopamine release in striosomes is especially engaged by aversive-predictive cues 15, the emerging picture is of a compartmental architecture in which striosomes and matrix may learn under partially different dopaminergic regimes even within the same striatal territory. This organization is consistent with–though does not by itself prove–the compartment-specific critic-versus-actor division of labor proposed in the loss-function section.

Taken together, the evidence reviewed in this subsection establishes that the basal ganglia’s plasticity rules are not a single canonical recipe applied uniformly across the striatum, but a family of regionally and compartmentally parameterized learning rules that share a common molecular toolkit—three-factor dopamine-gated Hebbian/anti-Hebbian STDP, endocannabinoid-dependent LTD, eligibility traces, cholinergic gating—but differ in their temporal profiles, polarity biases, pathway selectivity, and effective learning rates across striatal territories. In DMS, symmetric anti-Hebbian STDP, transient synaptic potentiation during early learning, and strong engagement of neuromodulatory gating favor rapid, flexible acquisition of goal-directed contingencies that can be readily overwritten when the environment changes. In DLS, asymmetric anti-Hebbian STDP, progressive and long-lasting potentiation concentrated in D2-expressing striatopallidal neurons, and slower formation of spatially clustered ensembles favor the consolidation of stable, extinction-resistant habits and motor skills. In ventral striatum, bidirectional plasticity from a single induction protocol, distinct calcium-signaling mechanisms, longer cholinergic plasticity windows, and morphologically specialized neuronal substrates favor the kind of rapid, flexible value estimation that the critic side of the actor–critic architecture requires. And at the striosome–matrix interface, opposite dopaminergic modulation of up-state dynamics and differential dopamine release produce compartment-specific learning rates that may support the separation of policy evaluation (striosome) from policy expression (matrix). The effective loss function that each territory optimizes is therefore matched, at the level of synaptic plasticity, by a learning rule whose parameterization is tuned to the computational demands of that territory’s position in the cortico-basal ganglia hierarchy. This is the synaptic-level instantiation of the broader principle established throughout this chapter: the basal ganglia do not implement a single optimizer with a single learning rule, but a structured portfolio of interacting optimizers, each with its own objective, its own error signal, and—as this section has shown—its own plasticity regime. A recent striatal model links dopamine-dependent plasticity and direct/indirect pathway activity to action selection and reinforcement learning (Figure).
